title: Middleware completed, no sales order
prompt: SAP Integration Suite shows the message as Completed, but no sales order exists in S/4HANA. Explain why the technical status is not enough and build the investigation.
expected_points: Start with stable message/business identity and correlation across sender, middleware and receiver.
Inspect whether the integration flow handled an exception in a way that can still end with Completed status.
Check receiver-side AIF/application logs and search for the business key or partial target object.
Determine whether the receiver committed, rejected, or never received the business event.
Close only after reconciling the source event with the target business document or an owned exception.
follow_up_questions: What if the receiver returned HTTP 200 but the response payload contains a business error?
Which business completion signal would you monitor proactively?
red_flags: Says Completed proves S/4 processed the order
Resends immediately without checking target commit

title: Timeout after possible receiver commit
prompt: A synchronous or asynchronous delivery times out after the receiver may already have committed the business object. The sender wants to retry immediately. Decide whether that is safe and explain the design you expect.
expected_points: Treat commit state as unknown until the target business key/object is checked.
Explain that guaranteed delivery or retry can redeliver the same event.
Require a stable semantic event ID and receiver/middleware duplicate handling or idempotency before blind retry.
If a durable side effect exists, use reconciliation or compensation rather than pretending the first attempt did not happen.
Define how retry identity and deduplication retention are controlled.
follow_up_questions: What happens after the deduplication retention window expires?
When would source replay be safer than middleware retry?
red_flags: Retries because the sender did not receive success
Generates a new event ID for the retry
Claims a queue alone guarantees exactly-once business effect

title: One qRFC LUW blocks thousands of successors
prompt: An outbound qRFC queue has one failed LUW at the front and thousands of later messages are waiting. Business asks you to release the queue immediately. Explain when restart or release is safe and when it is not.
expected_points: Read the exact qRFC status and error before changing queue state.
Identify whether the queue represents a real business ordering dependency or only transport serialization.
Understand the first failed LUW and target commit state before reactivation.
Explain that reactivation can duplicate processing if a supposedly running LUW is still active in the target.
Do not let successors overtake a predecessor when target state depends on chronology.
Define a business-priority escalation when one poison event blocks a high-value backlog.
follow_up_questions: How does SYSFAIL differ from a temporary retry state operationally?
Could you isolate the poison message into another flow without breaking business order?
red_flags: Deletes the first LUW to clear backlog
Activates every queue with no status interpretation
Optimizes throughput without checking business ordering

title: Deterministic validation error creates retry storm
prompt: A receiver rejects a message because mandatory master data is missing. Middleware retries it every few minutes, creating a growing alert and queue backlog. Design a better recovery pattern.
expected_points: Classify the failure as deterministic application/master-data error rather than transient transport failure.
Stop or bound automatic retries and route the poison message to an owned exception/quarantine path.
Preserve original identity, payload evidence and business priority while the master-data owner corrects the cause.
Restart or replay only after correction and verify the target business result.
Use backoff, retry thresholds and age/business-impact alerting for genuinely transient failures.
follow_up_questions: When would edit-and-restart in AIF be preferable to source replay?
What operational KPI would expose this failure before users complain?
red_flags: Drops the failed message and asks sender to recreate it later
Makes integration operations responsible for correcting all master data

title: IDoc reprocessing creates duplicate order
prompt: An inbound IDoc was in error, was reprocessed after a correction, and now the target contains two business documents for what users consider one event. Explain what was missing in the recovery contract.
expected_points: Inspect IDoc status history, payload and both target documents using the business key.
Determine whether the first attempt created a durable side effect before later status failure.
Explain that reprocessing the same technical message is not sufficient protection if target application processing is not idempotent.
Identify the stable business/event identity that should prevent or detect duplicate creation.
Define compensation/reversal for the duplicate and a safer restart contract for future incidents.
follow_up_questions: Would changing the IDoc number solve the architectural problem?
Where could duplicate protection live if the target application cannot implement it?
red_flags: Deletes one target document without reconciliation
Says BD87 caused the duplicate and stops there
Uses a new IDoc as the preferred fix for every error

title: Define integration operations KPIs
prompt: A program reports 99.9% technical message success but business teams still find missing and duplicate transactions. Define an operational scorecard that measures business integration health.
expected_points: Keep technical success rate but add source-to-target business reconciliation measures.
Track end-to-end latency from source event to durable target business state.
Measure failed/queued backlog by age, business priority and owner, not only raw count.
Track retry volume, retry age and duplicate/deduplication events.
Measure missing, duplicate and inconsistent business outcomes using business keys.
Include unowned exceptions and time-to-business-recovery as operational risk indicators.
follow_up_questions: Which KPI would best expose a green-but-missing-order problem?
How would you prioritize 20 blocked customer orders versus 50,000 successful master-data messages?
red_flags: Uses only availability and message success percentage
Measures middleware CPU as the main business KPI
